lead: A loop much smaller than a wavelength carries nearly the same current all the way round, so it behaves as a magnetic dipole: the same doughnut pattern as a short dipole, with E and H swapped. Its radiation resistance falls as the fourth power of size, so on medium wave a small loop radiates almost nothing and copper loss wins. Yet the same loop is the ferrite rod inside every AM radio and the sharp-null loop a direction finder turns to take a bearing.
prereq: You need: the Hertzian dipole and its sin θ pattern from Chapter 2.1, and radiation resistance and efficiency from Chapter 2.3.

blocks.text: A loop antenna is a conductor bent into a closed shape, fed so current runs round it. Its size is the circumference C = 2πa, where a is the loop radius in metres. The loop is small when C ≤ λ/10, with λ the wavelength in metres.

The limit comes from phase. A wave travelling round the wire makes the current at the far side lag the current at the near side. When C is under λ/10 the lag stays under 36°, so the current can be treated as one value I everywhere. A bigger loop carries a travelling wave and needs a different analysis.
With uniform current the loop reduces to one number, its magnetic moment m.

blocks.where: m is the magnetic moment in A·m²; N is the number of turns; I is the current in amperes, the same in every turn; A is the area enclosed by one turn in m². For a circular loop A = πa². The vector m points along the loop axis: curl the fingers of the right hand along the current and the thumb gives the direction.

blocks.text: The small loop is the twin of the short dipole. The dipole is an electric dipole — charge q pushed a distance d apart, moment qd. The loop is a magnetic dipole of moment m. Both have the same pattern and directivity, but E and H swap roles. N turns multiply m by N, because each turn carries the same current and adds its own area.
In the far field the small loop radiates only E_φ and H_θ; the short dipole radiates E_θ and H_φ. Swap one for the other and the dipole formulas carry over.
E_φ = 120π² (N I A) sin θ / (λ² r)
blocks.where: E_φ is the far electric field in V/m; θ is the angle measured from the loop axis; r is the distance in metres; 120π Ω is the impedance of free space. The magnetic field is H_θ = E_φ / 120π, in A/m. Both fall as 1/r, and the pattern is sin θ.

blocks.text: The pattern peaks in the plane of the loop and is zero along the axis, so the directivity is 1.5, that is 1.76 dBi, as for the short dipole. Pushing the power back through the field gives:

blocks.where: R_r is the radiation resistance in ohms; N is the number of turns; A is the loop area in m²; λ is the wavelength in metres. The constant 320π⁴ is about 31 171.

blocks.text: For a single-turn circular loop, putting A = C²/(4π) turns this into a formula in the circumference alone:

blocks.where: C is the circumference in metres and λ the wavelength in metres. Both forms agree; use whichever data you are given.

blocks.text: The fourth power is the whole story. A single turn of area 1 m² at λ = 30 m has R_r = 31 171 × (1/900)² = 0.038 Ω. Halve every dimension and the area drops four times while R_r drops sixteen times. Wire loss of a few tenths of an ohm then swamps radiation, and efficiency falls to a few per cent.

Medium-wave broadcast runs from about 530 kHz to 1.6 MHz, so λ lies between roughly 570 m and 190 m. Even a λ/10 loop would be several metres to nearly twenty metres across — impossible inside a radio set. The practical answer is a coil wound on a ferrite rod.

The rod concentrates flux, so the coil behaves as if its area were A_eff = μ_eff A, where μ_eff is the effective relative permeability of the rod. It is smaller than the material's own μ_r because the rod is short, but still tens to a few hundred. Since R_r goes as A², the rod raises the radiation resistance by μ_eff², while the open-circuit received voltage rises by only μ_eff, in proportion to the effective area A_eff = μ_eff A. The null lies along the rod's axis, which is why an AM radio is turned to put the rod broadside to the station.

The other everyday use is direction finding. The loop null is a true zero, and near it the pattern rises as sin θ ≈ θ, so a small rotation gives a large change in signal — a bearing to a degree or two. The deeper the null, the better the bearing; that sharpness, not gain, is the loop's real gift.

The pattern has two nulls 180° apart, so one loop cannot tell a station from its mirror image. A short vertical sense antenna, or a second loop at right angles, breaks the ambiguity. The loop impedance is small and inductive and is tuned by a capacitor; receive behaviour belongs to Chapter 2.7.

examples.question: A small loop has N = 10 turns of radius a = 0.1 m and works at 10 MHz. Its loss resistance is 0.05 Ω. Find the loop area, the radiation resistance and the radiation efficiency.
steps: Area of one turn: A = πa² = π × (0.1)² = 0.0314 m².
Size check: C = 2πa = 0.628 m and λ/10 = 3 m, so C < λ/10 and the loop is small.
Efficiency: η_rad = R_r / (R_r + R_loss) = 0.0038 / 0.0538 = 0.071, about 7 per cent.
examples.answer: A = 0.0314 m², R_r = 3.8 mΩ, and η_rad ≈ 0.07, about 7 per cent.
examples.check:
import math
a = 0.1
N = 10
f = 10e6
c = 3e8
R_loss = 0.05
A = math.pi * a**2
lam = c / f
x = N * A / lam**2
Rr = 320 * math.pi**4 * x**2
eta = Rr / (Rr + R_loss)
print(round(A, 6))
print(round(lam, 1))
print(round(x, 6))
print(round(Rr, 6))
print(round(eta, 4))

traps: Squaring only the area and dropping N, giving R_r too small by N². The number of turns sits inside the bracket and is squared with everything else.

Using the wire radius, or the diameter, where the loop radius belongs in A = πa². A diameter used as radius makes the area four times too large, and after squaring makes R_r sixteen times too large; using the wire radius makes it far too small.
Confusing the two nulls: the short dipole is null along the wire, the small loop along its axis, broadside to the plane of the loop. Examiners ask for the pattern sketch to catch this.
Applying the small-loop formula when C is a large fraction of λ. The current is then not uniform, R_r is far larger, and the sin θ pattern fails.
Mixing units — area in cm² or λ in cm. Both must be in metres, because the constant 31 171 assumes SI.

quiz.q: State the condition for a loop antenna to be treated as small, and say what it guarantees about the current.
quiz.a: C ≤ λ/10. It guarantees the current is nearly uniform in amplitude and phase all round the loop.

quiz.q: Write the magnetic moment of an N-turn loop and give its unit and direction.
quiz.a: m = NIA, in A·m², pointing along the loop axis by the right-hand rule with the fingers along the current.

quiz.q: Why is the small loop called a magnetic dipole, and how do its far fields differ from those of a short electric dipole?
quiz.a: Its far field is that of a magnetic moment. The loop radiates E_φ and H_θ; the short dipole radiates E_θ and H_φ. Pattern shape, sin θ dependence and directivity 1.5 are identical; only the field components are exchanged.

quiz.q: A single-turn circular loop of radius 0.5 m works at 10 MHz. Find its radiation resistance. Is the small-loop formula valid here?
quiz.a: λ = 30 m, C = 2π × 0.5 = 3.14 m, just over λ/10 = 3 m, so the formula is marginal — say so. A = 0.785 m². NA/λ² = 8.73 × 10⁻⁴. R_r = 31 171 × (8.73 × 10⁻⁴)² = 0.024 Ω.

quiz.q: A 20-turn loop of radius 0.05 m works at 30 MHz with a loss resistance of 0.1 Ω. Find the radiation resistance and the efficiency.
quiz.a: λ = 10 m, C = 0.314 m < 1 m, so the loop is small. A = 7.85 × 10⁻³ m². NA/λ² = 1.57 × 10⁻³. R_r = 0.077 Ω. η_rad = 0.077/(0.077 + 0.1) = 0.43, about 43 per cent.

quiz.q: Explain why the radiation resistance of a small loop falls as the fourth power of its size, and what this means for a medium-wave receiver antenna.
quiz.a: The far field is proportional to m = NIA, so radiated power and hence R_r go as A². Since A goes as the square of a linear dimension, R_r goes as that dimension to the fourth power. At medium wave λ is hundreds of metres, so an air loop would have R_r far below its copper loss; a ferrite core must multiply the effective area before the antenna is useful.

quiz.q: Why is a loop null good for direction finding, and how is the 180° ambiguity removed?
quiz.a: The null is a true zero and the pattern behaves as sin θ ≈ θ near it, so a one-degree turn produces a large fractional change in signal; the bearing can be read to a degree or two. The two nulls are 180° apart, so a sense antenna or a second loop at right angles decides which null points at the transmitter.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same physics runs contactless cards and phone payments: an NFC or RFID reader at 13.56 MHz drives a small loop whose near field couples inductively into the tag, so the tag needs no battery. Wireless phone charging and induction hobs use coupled loops at higher power. In research, electrically small antennas are limited by the Chu–Harrington bound, which ties bandwidth to size. Search for electrically small antennas, the Chu limit, and ferrite rod permeability to go further.
